title: Every file upload 500s in the launch configuration: the unlimited storage quota overflows Postgres bigint
what: `unlimitedPlan()` substitutes `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` for every int feature while billing is off. `StorageService.put` computes `limitBytes = BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n` = 9444732965739289378816 and binds it into a raw `UPDATE tenants ... AND "storageUsedBytes" + $n <= $limitBytes`. Prisma binds it as int8; the value is ~1024x the bigint maximum, so Postgres rejects with SQLSTATE 22003. The throw is outside the try/catch, which only wraps `driver.put` at line 103.
impact: With subscriptions off — the launch configuration — no tenant can upload a book cover, member photo, branding logo, PDF attachment or MARC file. Every attempt is an opaque HTTP 500. Turning billing ON is what makes it work, the opposite of what an operator would guess.
evidence: READ: effective-plan.service.ts:38 `const UNLIMITED_INT = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;`, line 52 assigns it to every int feature, line 110-111 applies `unlimitedPlan` whenever `settings.billingEnabled()` is false. features.ts:44-51 confirms `max_storage_mb` is type 'int', so `getInt` returns the sentinel unchanged. config/env.ts:366 `billingEnabled: bool('BILLING_ENABLED', false)` and .env.prod.example:65 `BILLING_ENABLED=false` confirm the launch default.
verification: Re-derived independently rather than trusting the original probe. RAN `psql -d libriant_control -c "SELECT 9007199254740991::bigint * 1024 * 1024"` -> `ERROR: bigint out of range`. Then RAN the EXACT `controlDb.$executeRaw` template from storage.service.ts:74-79 against the live audit control plane with `limitBytes = BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) * 1024n * 1024n` and a real tenant id -> `PrismaClientKnownRequestError ... Raw query failed. Code: 22003. Message: value "9444732965739289378816" is out of range for type bigint`. The claim that Prisma binds the BigInt as int8 (rather than numeric, which would not overflow) is the load-bearing step and it holds. Severity upheld: this is not a race or an edge case — it is 100% of uploads in the configuration the product ships in.
fix: Treat the sentinel as 'no ceiling' in StorageService: `const unlimited = limitMb >= Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;` and run the UPDATE without the `<=` predicate when true. Alternatively clamp UNLIMITED_INT at effective-plan.service.ts:38 to a value whose byte product fits int8 (e.g. 2**43 MB). Add an integration test with BILLING_ENABLED=false that uploads a cover — apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts:8 forces `BILLING_ENABLED ||= 'true'`, so the whole suite runs in the opposite configuration from production.

title: Re-importing a file after a failure silently duplicates every row without a natural key, including patrons' fines
what: The engine's idempotency contract only covers rows that HAVE a natural key it looks up. `commitFine` is a bare `fine.create` with no dedupe and `loanId` left NULL, so the `fines_one_outstanding_per_loan` partial unique index (which is `WHERE status='outstanding' AND "loanId" IS NOT NULL`) never applies. `commitBook` dedupes only on `isbn13`. `commitMember` dedupes only on memberNumber or email. `commitLoan` blocks only a duplicate ACTIVE loan. `commitReservation` relies on `reservations_one_active_per_book_member`, which is `WHERE status IN ('queued','ready')` only. Nothing records per-row progress, so any second pass over the file re-commits everything.
impact: A librarian whose 20,000-row import dies at row 12,000 has one obvious action: send the file again. Doing so doubles every already-committed fine, every ISBN-less book, every closed loan, every number-less member and every resolved hold. Patrons are billed twice with no marker distinguishing the duplicate. There is no de-duplication tool and no undo. Bulk import is the onboarding path for every new library.
evidence: RAN the real `ImportEngine` twice over the same one-row payload against the live tenant DB with duplicateMode='skip' (the safest setting): fine imported twice -> `FINES rows = 2 total cents = 1000` for a file that said 500c; ISBN-less book imported twice -> `ISBN-LESS BOOKS = 2`. Both passes returned outcome 'imported' with zero issues. READ: the `fines_one_outstanding_per_loan` index at packages/db-tenant/prisma/migrations/20260614000000_fine_one_outstanding_per_loan/migration.sql:36-38 is conditioned on `"loanId" IS NOT NULL`, and commitFine's create at import-engine.ts:683-694 never sets loanId.
verification: Reproduced the two sharpest sub-claims end-to-end (see evidence). Then attacked the framing: the original finding hangs the harm on `requireRunnable` (import.service.ts:332-345) letting a 'failed' batch be re-run. I checked whether that route is actually reachable and found the UI does NOT expose it — ImportWizard.tsx:61 lists 'failed' as TERMINAL and line 264 renders DonePanel, whose only action is `onAgain={reset}` (start over with a fresh upload). This does not kill the finding; it makes it worse. The realistic recovery is re-uploading the same file as a NEW batch, which duplicates identically, and there is no file-level dedupe (grep for checksum/sha256/hash in import.service.ts and import-staging.ts returns nothing), so an accidental double upload has the same effect. The crash-recovery sweep (import-queue.service.ts:103-158) sets wedged batches to 'failed' but does not auto re-run, so no unattended amplification. Severity upheld at high: silent financial duplication on the onboarding path, reachable by ordinary user action, with no undo.
fix: Persist per-row progress: record `(batchId, rowNumber) -> entityId` inside the same commit as the row and skip already-recorded rows on any re-run of that batch. Independently, give the fine/loan/reservation committers a natural key (e.g. a stable `importBatchId + rowNumber` marker column with a unique index) so a fresh re-upload of the same file cannot double-write. Until then, change the UI copy on a failed import from an implicit 'try again' to an explicit warning that re-importing duplicates rows already written.

title: `books.isbn13` has no unique constraint, yet the import treats it as the natural key for skip/update
what: The import's dedupe is `findFirst({ where: { isbn13, archivedAt: null } })` with nothing behind it — the only ISBN objects in the schema are a non-unique btree index and the `books_isbn13_shape` digits CHECK. `BooksService.create` performs no ISBN lookup at all. Two book rows with the same ISBN-13 are therefore trivially reachable, after which `findBookByIsbn` returns an arbitrary one, so `duplicateMode:'update'` refreshes a coin-flip row and `resolveBook` attaches imported copies, loans and holds to a coin-flip row.
impact: The catalogue splits: the same title appears twice, its copies land under one entry and its holds under the other, and a re-import updates whichever row Postgres returns first. There is no merge tool, so the cleanup is manual re-pointing of copies.
evidence: RAN four `ImportEngine` instances committing the same isbn13 '9781234567897' concurrently against the live tenant DB -> `D) books with SAME isbn13 = 4`. Then RAN a direct `book.create` with the same ISBN (the shape BooksService.create writes) -> `E) after manual create, books with SAME isbn13 = 5`. READ: migration 20260526184041_init:305 `CREATE INDEX "books_isbn13_idx"` — non-unique; books.service.ts:206-234 writes `isbn13` inside the quota transaction with no preceding lookup.
verification: Mechanism reproduced exactly as claimed — both the concurrent-import route and the manual-create route. The DOWNGRADE is on severity, not substance. Three reasons the stated harm does not reach 'high': (a) the damage is catalogue quality, not data or money loss — nothing is destroyed and every duplicate is visible in search rather than 'invisible until a patron cannot find a book'; (b) it is repairable by hand today (re-point copies, archive the spare) whereas the high-rated findings have no user-side recovery; (c) it is the identical mechanism as data-integrity-06 (authors), which the same auditor rated medium — one of the two ratings has to move, and the author case is if anything the more reachable of the pair. Also worth noting for the fix: a hard unique index on isbn13 may be wrong for libraries that keep separate bibliographic records per edition, so the constraint decision is a product question, not a pure bug fix.
fix: Decide whether ISBN is a key. If yes: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX books_isbn13_unique_active ON books(isbn13) WHERE isbn13 IS NOT NULL AND "archivedAt" IS NULL;` (matching book_copies_barcode_unique_active at migration 20260526184041_init:470) and translate the resulting P2002 into the existing 'duplicate' path in both `BooksService.create` and `ImportEngine.commitBook`. If no: stop using isbn13 as the import's natural key and match on a composite the library controls.

title: Imported `ready` holds are permanently unfulfillable, never expire, and freeze renewals on that title
what: `commitReservation` writes a status='ready' hold with `readyAt` set but `fulfilledByCopyId` left null and no copy flipped to 'reserved'. Three downstream paths assume a ready hold owns a copy: `LoansService.checkout` refuses the pickup because `reservation.fulfilledByCopyId !== input.copyId` (loans.service.ts:269-273); `ReservationsService.resolveReservation` only frees a copy when `fulfilledByCopyId` is set; and the expiry sweep selects on `expiresAt: { lt: now }` (reservation-expiry.job.ts:92-95), which never matches when the import file carried no expiry date.
impact: The hold is immortal. It occupies the `reservations_one_active_per_book_member` slot so that member can never re-hold the book, and `LoansService.renew` (loans.service.ts:621-631) refuses every renewal of that title for every member while any queued/ready hold exists. Importing an existing library's hold list — the entire purpose of the reservation importer — wedges renewals on each affected title until a staff member finds and cancels each hold by hand. The patron is also emailed 'your hold is ready' for a book they cannot collect.
evidence:
RAN the real ImportEngine on one reservation row with status='ready' against the live tenant DB, with one 'available' copy of the book present:
  outcome imported []
  reservation: {"status":"ready","readyAt":"2026-08-23T10:14:01.034Z","expiresAt":null,"fulfilledByCopyId":null,"queuePosition":null}
  copy status: available
  expiry sweep would match (status=ready AND expiresAt < far-future): 0
verification: Reproduced verbatim — the orphan ready hold, the untouched copy, and the sweep matching zero rows even against a far-future cutoff. Checked each downstream claim in source rather than taking them on trust: loans.service.ts:269-273 does compare `fulfilledByCopyId !== input.copyId` and throws, so null blocks every pickup; loans.service.ts:621-631 does throw on any reservation in status queued|ready for the book, so renewals are genuinely frozen; reservation-expiry.job.ts:92-95 does filter on `expiresAt: { lt: now }`, and a null expiresAt is never `< now` in Postgres, so the sweep can never reach it. The one moderating fact — a file that DOES carry an expiry date escapes the immortality half — is already acknowledged in the finding. Severity upheld at medium: no data is lost and staff can cancel the hold, but the wedge is silent, self-inflicted by the documented migration path, and scales with the size of the imported hold list.
fix: In `commitReservation`, for status='ready' take the same `book:<bookId>` advisory lock the other allocation paths use, claim a copy with a CAS (`bookCopy.updateMany where status='available'`), set `fulfilledByCopyId`, and default `expiresAt` to `now + holdPickupHours` when the file has none. If no copy is free, downgrade the row to 'queued' with a warning issue rather than writing an orphan ready hold.

title: `authors.sortName` has no unique constraint, so the import's advertised author de-duplication is unenforced
what: The engine header (import-engine.ts:10-11) promises 'authors are find-or-created by normalized name so a catalogue import doesn't spawn duplicate author rows', implemented as `findFirst({ where: { sortName } })` then `create`. Nothing backs it: there is no unique index on `sortName` (only a btree and a trgm gin index), and `AuthorsService.create` at line 72 is a bare `client.author.create` with no lookup, so the UI happily creates the same author twice. Once two rows share a sortName, every later `findAuthorId` returns an arbitrary one.
impact: The author's bibliography splits across two rows permanently: browsing by author shows the name twice, each holding a subset of the books, with no merge tool. Because Greek names are accent-folded into `sortName`, near-identical spellings collapse to the same key, so the split is invisible in the UI until a patron searches.
evidence: RAN four concurrent ImportEngine instances each committing a book naming the same author -> `C) authors for one sortName = 4`, with the four rows sharing sortName 'nikos kazantzakis race' and four distinct ids. READ: authors.service.ts:72-82 creates unconditionally; migration 20260526184041_init:566 is `CREATE INDEX "authors_sortname_trgm" ... USING gin` and there is no unique index on authors anywhere in the migration set.
verification: Reproduced. Checked the two obvious refutations and neither holds: the engine's in-memory `authorCache` (import-engine.ts:110) does dedupe within a single run, and the import worker is `concurrency: 1` platform-wide (import-worker.ts:263) so two imports cannot race each other — but `AuthorsService.create` needs no concurrency at all to produce the duplicate, and that is the realistic route (a librarian adds the author manually, then imports a catalogue naming them). Severity upheld at medium: quality damage, visible, hand-repairable, no loss.
fix: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX authors_sortname_unique_active ON authors("sortName") WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL;` and convert `findOrCreateAuthor` to an upsert on that key (catch P2002, re-read). Give `AuthorsService.create` the same lookup so the UI returns the existing author instead of a second row.

title: The import pipeline enforces `max_books`/`max_members` from a private in-memory counter outside the advisory-lock domain every other path uses
what: Every other create path routes through `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx` (quota.service.ts:62-65), which takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('quota:<tenant>:<feature>:<ctx>')` as the first statement of the caller's transaction and counts inside it. The import engine does not join that lock domain: `init()` snapshots the live count once, resolves the limit once via `ctx.getLimit`, and then decides per row from `this.quotaUsed`. The API process and the worker enforce the same ceiling against two non-communicating views.
impact: A tenant can end up over its plan ceiling by roughly the number of manual creates that land during an import. No data is corrupted and nothing is billed wrongly — plans are flat-rate, not usage-metered — so the practical cost is a tenant sitting a handful of rows above a limit until someone notices.
evidence: READ: import-engine.ts:143-152 seeds `quotaUsed` from a single `count()` in `init()`; line 152 resolves `quotaLimit` once; `quotaBlocked` at 203-215 compares only against those two in-memory fields; the only `pg_advisory_xact_lock` in the file is at line 651 for reservation queue positions. Contrast quota.service.ts:62-65, which is the locked path all ten UI call sites use.
verification: The mechanism is real and I confirmed it by reading — but the severity and most of the stated impact do not survive. (1) The finding calls the overshoot 'unbounded in principle'. It is not: the import worker runs `concurrency: 1` platform-wide (import-worker.ts:263), so no second import can race, and the engine's own counter still stops it at the ceiling. The only writers that can slip past are manual UI creates landing inside the import window — bounded by staff throughput, i.e. single digits. (2) The finding's 'sharp reading' — that libraries will load catalogues of arbitrary size today and be silently over quota when billing flips on — is NOT caused by this bug. That is caused by `unlimitedPlan` (effective-plan.service.ts:46-57) raising every int limit to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for EVERY path while billing is off; fixing the import's lock domain would change nothing about it. Attributing that consequence here inflates the finding. (3) Nothing is corrupted and nobody is under-billed, because subscriptions are flat-rate per plan rather than per row. Downgraded from high to low: a real architectural inconsistency worth closing, not something that wakes anyone.
fix: Have `commitBook`/`commitMember` call `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx` inside the same `$transaction` as the row insert, on the same `quota:<tenantId>:<featureKey>` key the UI uses, and delete the `quotaUsed`/`quotaLimit` fields. Cost is one advisory lock per imported row on a key that only serialises import rows against each other, which is free given concurrency 1.

title: Member archive and hold placement use different lock domains, so a member can be archived while acquiring a live hold
what: `MembersService.archive` takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('member:<id>')` and counts open loans AND active reservations inside that transaction. That serialises correctly against `LoansService.checkout`, which takes the same member lock and re-reads the member inside its own transaction. `ReservationsService.place` does neither: it validates `member.archivedAt` / `member.status` at lines 106-122 OUTSIDE any transaction, and its transaction (line 195) takes only `book:<bookId>`. The two paths never mutually exclude.
impact: Produces exactly the state `archive()` exists to prevent — an archived member holding a live hold, which occupies the `reservations_one_active_per_book_member` slot and blocks renewals of that title for everyone. If the queue later promotes it, a physical copy flips to 'reserved' for a member who no longer exists and is stranded until staff cancel the hold by hand.
evidence: READ: reservations.service.ts:106-122 reads and validates the member with a plain `client.member.findUnique` before any transaction is opened; the transaction at line 182-195 issues only `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('book:<bookId>', 0))`. members.service.ts:443 takes `member:<id>` and never touches the book lock. Compare loans.service.ts:229-238, which does take the member lock and re-read inside the transaction — the reservation path is the odd one out.
verification: Mechanism confirmed by reading both transaction bodies; the asymmetry with the loans path is exactly as described. Downgraded from medium to low on reachability: the window is the ~5 round-trips between the member read at line 108 and the transaction commit, on the order of tens of milliseconds, and it requires an archive and a hold placement for the SAME member to collide inside it — two operations a library performs a handful of times a day. The end state is also recoverable without support (staff cancel the hold), unlike the findings above it. Separately, while checking this I found a wider non-race route to the same end state that is NOT part of this finding and belongs to whoever owns the import dimension: `findMemberByNumber` at import-engine.ts:765-773 omits the `archivedAt: null` filter that `findMemberByEmail` at 782-784 has, so importing a reservation keyed on an archived member's number attaches a live hold to an archived member with no concurrency at all.
fix: In `ReservationsService.place`, take `pg_advisory_xact_lock('member:<memberId>')` alongside the existing `book:<bookId>` lock at the top of the transaction and re-read the member's status/archivedAt inside it, mirroring loans.service.ts:229-238. Acquire the two locks in a fixed order (member then book) in both services to avoid deadlock.

title: tenant-relocate lifts the source database's read-only fence before the control-plane cutover and cache bust
what: The script fences the SOURCE database with `ALTER DATABASE ... SET default_transaction_read_only = on` because (its own comment, lines 118-124) admin/impersonation routes and background workers bypass the HTTP read_only middleware and their writes would be excluded from the snapshot. It then lifts that fence at lines 164-172 — before `tenant.dbUrl` is updated (176), before the resolver cache is busted (202) and before the read_only window is closed (205). For that interval the tenant still resolves to the source and the source is writable again.
impact: A background sweep firing in that interval writes to a database that is about to be abandoned; those writes are already outside the pg_dump and are lost at cutover, with no reconciliation step.
evidence: READ scripts/tenant-relocate.ts. Success-path order is pg_dump (136) -> pg_restore (148) -> verifyDestination (155) -> unfenceSource (165) -> control-plane dbUrl update (176) -> bustResolverCache (202) -> closeEvent (205). The comment at 157-162 justifies the early unfence as 'the source is no longer referenced', but at line 165 the control plane still points every request at it.
verification: The ordering claim is exactly right and I confirmed it line by line. Half the stated impact is refuted, and the other half is far narrower than presented. Refuted: 'the same applies to any API process still holding a cached tenant client after the cutover' — `TenantPrismaService.getClient` (tenant-prisma.service.ts:63-74) compares the cached entry's `dbUrl` against the resolved context and rebuilds the client whenever it differs, and the tenant context itself comes from a Redis-backed resolver cache (tenant-resolver.service.ts:106-107) which `bustResolverCache` (tenant-relocate.ts:457-468) deletes, so there is no per-process straggler holding the old URL. Narrowed: the genuine exposure is lines 165 to 202 — one control-plane transaction plus a Redis DEL, tens of milliseconds — and HTTP writes are still blocked by the read_only system mode throughout (closed only at 205), so only a cron worker firing in that exact instant can hit it. Downgraded from medium to low. Worth noting for whoever fixes it: `ALTER DATABASE ... SET` only applies to NEW sessions, so pooled worker connections opened before `fenceSourceReadOnly` are never fenced at all — the ordering is the smaller of the two problems with this fence.
fix: Move the `unfenceSource` call below `closeEvent(modeEvent.id)` and after a drain interval equal to the resolver cache TTL, so the DB-level fence is the last thing removed rather than the first. Keep the failure-path unfence at line 214 where it belongs. Separately, terminate or recycle source connections when fencing, since ALTER DATABASE does not affect open sessions.

title: Stripe subscription webhooks do multi-statement read-modify-write with no transaction or row lock
what: `syncStripeSubscription` reads the current subscription (582), derives `graceUntil` from what it read (630-637), then writes (614) and writes again (643) — four round-trips on the shared `controlDb` client with no `$transaction` and no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. The controller's Redis SETNX dedupes by `event.id` only, so it serialises retries of ONE event but never two distinct events for the same tenant. The stale-replay guard at 601-612 compares `current_period_start`, which is identical for events inside one billing period, so it does not order same-period events.
impact: A lost update on a subscription row: a concurrently-processing event can overwrite a `graceUntil` or `status` another handler just wrote, leaving a paid tenant marked past_due or a delinquent tenant with an open grace window until the next event corrects it.
evidence: READ: billing.service.ts:582 `const existing = await controlDb.subscription.findUnique(...)` and 614 `await controlDb.subscription.update(...)` are separate statements with no wrapper; stripe-webhook.controller.ts:90-96 keys the SETNX on `EVENT_KEY(event.id)`; the dispatch switch at 126-151 takes no per-tenant lock in any branch.
verification: The read-modify-write and the event-id-scoped dedupe are both exactly as described. Downgraded from medium to low on three counts. (1) Unreachable in the shipping configuration: BILLING_ENABLED=false, STRIPE_DRIVER=fake and every price ID is a `price_seed_*` placeholder, so no real Stripe event reaches this code on Monday — it is a latent risk for whenever billing is switched on, which is the right framing for a launch audit. (2) It needs two DISTINCT events for the same tenant to be in flight simultaneously AND to interleave between the read at 582 and the write at 614 — a sub-round-trip window. (3) It is self-correcting: the whole subscription row is re-derived from the payload on every subsequent `customer.subscription.*` event, and Stripe emits those liberally, so a wrong `graceUntil` is overwritten by the next event rather than persisting. The finding's phrase 'directly gates or ungates features for real money' is true of the value but overstates its durability. Confidence on the mechanism is high; confidence that it ever produces a customer-visible wrong state is low.
fix: Wrap each handler body in `controlDb.$transaction` opened with `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('billing:' || tenantId, 0))` — the pattern StaffService.create already uses against the control plane. Additionally persist the Stripe event `created` timestamp on the subscription row and refuse any event older than the last applied one, which orders same-period events that the `current_period_start` guard cannot.

title: `audit_log_retention_days` is priced across five plan tiers but enforced nowhere
what: The tenant schema comment at schema.prisma:563 states retention is 'governed by the tenant's plan (`audit_log_retention_days` feature) and enforced by a background job', and the repricing migration writes five distinct values (7 / 90 / 365 / 1095 / 3650 days). No such job exists, and no read path applies the limit either.
impact: The retention ladder is a phantom differentiator — every tenant keeps unlimited history regardless of plan — and `audit_log` grows without pruning in every tenant database, inflating each pg_dump, relocate and DR restore.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn audit_log_retention_days apps packages scripts` (excluding node_modules and dist) returns only the feature definition at features.ts:113, the six seed values at seed-data.ts:96/126/157/188/218/249, the six migration inserts in 20260822140000_repricing/migration.sql, one site copy reference at apps/site/src/plans.ts:231, and the schema comment — no consumer anywhere. apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts registers nine jobs (support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications, storage-temp-cleanup); none touches audit_log.
verification: The absence is real and I re-derived it independently — the grep returns definitions and seed values only, and the registry list is complete. Downgraded from medium to low because the impact is weaker than stated in every branch. Commercially it is under-delivery in the customer's favour: nobody is harmed by getting more history than they paid for, and no customer can detect it. Operationally, the growth estimate does not hold up for the target workload — a Greek municipal library generating a few thousand auditable changes a month adds single-digit MB a year, which is noise next to the catalogue and cover storage in the same dump. And with BILLING_ENABLED=false, `unlimitedPlan` raises this int to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for every tenant anyway, so even a shipped job would prune nothing at launch. This is a docs-vs-reality gap and a pricing-page accuracy question, not a data-integrity hazard. The GDPR angle raised in the original impact is out of this dimension and should be judged by the privacy-legal reviewer.
fix: Either add an `audit-log-retention` job to the registry that resolves the feature per active tenant and deletes older `audit_log` rows in bounded batches, or remove the enforcement claim from schema.prisma:563 and the retention row from the pricing page until it ships.

title: Member-number generation runs outside the transaction whose lock its comment claims serialises it
what: The comment at 221-226 says the quota advisory lock 'also serializes member-number assignment'. It does not: `nextSequenceForYear(client, year)` is called at line 249 on the base client, before `createWithQuota` opens the transaction that takes the lock. Concurrent creates read the same max and collide on `members_member_number_unique_active`; the loop at 247 absorbs at most three attempts before surfacing an error. `nextSequenceForYear` (member-numbers.ts:36-50) also loads every member number for the year into memory with an unbounded `findMany`.
impact: With several staff enrolling members at the same moment — a school or municipal enrolment day — a legitimate signup can fail with a 'member number already exists' conflict the librarian never caused. The full scan per attempt also makes each retry slower as the member table grows, widening the collision window rather than narrowing it.
evidence: READ: members.service.ts:249 `const seq = await nextSequenceForYear(client, year);` sits in the retry loop at 247, outside the `client.$transaction` that `createWithQuota` (227-237) opens. member-numbers.ts:8-12 acknowledges the race and prescribes a retry limit of 3, which line 247 implements as `attempt < 3`. member-numbers.ts:40-43 is `findMany` selecting every matching memberNumber with no limit or aggregate.
verification: Confirmed by reading the call ordering: `nextSequenceForYear` takes the base `client`, not the `tx`, and is invoked before `createWithQuota` is called, so no lock is held when the max is read. The comment is simply wrong. Checked whether the retry loop rescues it and it only partly does — each retry re-reads the max, so it converges, but three attempts is a small budget and the error surfaced on exhaustion is `translateCreateError(lastErr)`, i.e. the duplicate-member-number conflict, which is confusing when the librarian typed no number. Severity upheld at low: the collision needs genuine simultaneity, it fails closed (no bad data is written), and the librarian can simply retry.
fix: Move the `nextSequenceForYear` call inside `createWithQuota`'s transaction, after `enforceWithinTx` has taken the `quota:<tenant>:max_members` lock — the number is then assigned under the same serialisation as the insert and the retry loop becomes dead code. Replace the `findMany` with a `SELECT max(...)` over the numeric tail, or keep a per-year sequence row.

title: The nightly `storageUsedBytes` recompute that three code comments name as the drift backstop does not exist
what: `StorageService` maintains a cached byte counter on `tenants.storageUsedBytes` and, at three separate points, justifies best-effort error handling by deferring to a recompute that is never scheduled: line 30 'run nightly in prod', line 113 'the nightly recompute (and `recomputeUsage` below) is the backstop', line 189 'a failure leaves the counter high until the nightly recompute'. `recomputeUsage` (line 208) has exactly one non-test caller.
impact: Every swallowed `releaseReservedBytes` failure (the `.catch` at 199-204 logs and continues) and every driver/DB divergence is permanent. The drift is one-directional — the counter only ever sticks high — so a tenant progressively loses usable storage until uploads return 402 citing a usage figure that does not match what is on disk, with no operator command to correct it.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn recomputeUsage apps scripts` (excluding node_modules/dist) returns the definition at storage.service.ts:208, the three comments at 30/113/189, one unrelated mention in quota-counters.ts:44 and local-driver.ts:177, and exactly one call site: storage-demo.controller.ts:181. apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts registers nine jobs, including `storage-temp-cleanup`, but nothing that calls recomputeUsage.
verification: Re-derived the grep independently; the single demo-controller call site is the whole of it, and the registry list is complete. Checked that the drift direction claim holds: `releaseReservedBytes` (188-204) is the only decrement path and its failure is swallowed by `.catch`, while the reservation at 74-79 is a hard `$executeRaw` whose failure propagates — so the counter can be left high but never low, exactly as claimed. Severity upheld at low: it takes repeated control-plane write failures to accumulate meaningful drift, and the failure mode is a conservative over-count rather than a quota bypass. Note the interaction with data-integrity-01 — while billing is off no upload succeeds at all, so no drift accrues until that is fixed.
fix: Register a nightly `storage-usage-recompute` job that walks active tenants and calls `recomputeUsage`, or delete the three comments and make `releaseReservedBytes` failures loud instead of best-effort.

title: The reservation-expiry sweep stamps promotions with a clock captured before the loop, which can trip the `reservations_ready_after_placed` CHECK
what: `const now = new Date()` is taken once per tenant at line 90, above the overdue query at 92 and the loop at 105. Line 173 writes `readyAt: now` on the promoted hold. A hold placed after that instant but promoted in this pass has `placedAt > now`, and `reservations_ready_after_placed` (migration 20260526184041_init:521-522) requires `readyAt >= placedAt`. The service paths take a fresh `new Date()` inside their transactions.
impact: The promotion transaction aborts with a CHECK violation, is caught and logged, and that one hold's expiry is deferred to the next sweep 60 seconds later.
evidence: READ. reservation-expiry.job.ts:90 `const now = new Date();`; line 173 `readyAt: now` inside the `promotedNext` updateMany; migration 20260526184041_init:521-522 `CHECK ("readyAt" IS NULL OR "readyAt" >= "placedAt")`. Compare reservations.service.ts:501, which takes `now` inside `promoteNextHoldInTx`.
verification: The stale-clock mechanism is real, and the trigger is narrower than described but reachable: `next` is selected `orderBy: queuePosition asc`, i.e. the queue HEAD, so a just-placed hold only qualifies when it is the sole queued hold — which does happen, because the expiring hold's copy is still 'reserved' at placement time so `place()` queues rather than auto-promotes. The stated impact, however, is wrong on the load-bearing clause. The finding says the copy 'stays stranded in reserved until the next run — which fails the same way if the queue head is still the newer hold'. It does not: the failure is caught per-reservation at line 200-202 (`logger.warn`), the job is registered at `intervalMs: 60_000` (registry.ts:30-33), and each run calls `new Date()` afresh at line 90 — so on the next pass `now` is later than the newer hold's `placedAt` and the promotion succeeds. Total harm is a copy held one extra minute and one warning line. Downgraded from low to info: a real defect worth a one-line fix, but it should not compete for attention with anything above it.
fix: Take a fresh `const now = new Date()` inside the per-reservation transaction and use it for `readyAt`/`expiresAt`, keeping the outer `now` only for the `expiresAt < now` selection predicate.

title: Verified sound: the advisory-lock quota strategy holds wherever `enforceWithinTx` is actually used
where: apps/api/src/customization/quota.service.ts:49-65; call sites in catalog/books.service.ts:201,357, members/members.service.ts:229,362, customization/collections.service.ts:111,212,289, customization/collection-records.service.ts:98, customization/field-definitions.service.ts:130, staff/staff.service.ts:73-109
what: Recorded so the gaps above are read in proportion. `enforceWithinTx` takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('quota:<tenant>:<feature>:<context>', 0))` as the first statement of the caller's transaction and counts inside it, so the count and the insert observe a serialised view per quota key. Un-archive paths re-charge a seat, closing the archive-then-restore bypass, and control-plane `staff_seats` reimplements the same pattern against `controlDb`.
impact: None — this is the control that the import pipeline (data-integrity-04) and the storage path bypass, and it is worth knowing it works before anyone rewrites it.
evidence: READ quota.service.ts:61-65: the lock key is built first, `tx.$executeRaw` takes the advisory lock, then `input.count()` runs against the same `tx`, then `assertWithinLimit` throws the 402. Every call site passes the transaction client into `count`.
verification: Spot-checked the implementation rather than the original probe: quota.service.ts:62-63 does issue the advisory lock as the first statement, and the doc comment's contract at lines 47-48 matches the code. Kept as info — it is the reference pattern for fixing data-integrity-04 and its presence stops a reader concluding that quota enforcement is broken generally.
